phonemes.desc: Voiceless alveolar stop [t], plain and unaspirated as Welsh stops are, followed by a short open [a]; the first syllable is light and unstressed.
Voiced alveolar lateral [l] — the ordinary Welsh l, not the voiceless fricative ll [ɬ]; Taliesin keeps the soft single lateral.
The stressed penult [jɛs]: a palatal glide into open-mid [ɛ], sounding exactly like English 'yes'; Welsh accent falls on the penultimate syllable.
Short close [ɪ] and a final alveolar nasal [n], lightly sounded — Welsh final syllables are never swallowed.

pronunciation.approximation: 'tal-YES-in' — three syllables, the weight squarely on the middle one, the first a soft tap; exactly the living Welsh name.

kin.form: Taliesin — the spelling of the Book of Taliesin (NLW Peniarth MS 2), unchanged into modern Welsh.

kin.label: Historia Brittonum
kin.form: Taliesin, named among the five poets famed in the time of Ida of Bernicia — the name's oldest surviving notice.

kin.label: Welsh Triads
kin.form: Taliesin Ben Beirdd, 'Taliesin Chief of Bards', head of the Primary Chief Bards of the Isle of Britain.

kin.label: Etymology
kin.form: tal, 'forehead, brow' + iesin, 'radiant, shining' — the traditional gloss 'radiant brow', as discussed by Ifor Williams.

pronunciation.note: Taliesin is Tier 2 by the mechanical rule: medieval Welsh writes the name in plain Latin letters — no diacritic, no distinctive letter for the ASCII alphabet to lose. The name's fame vastly outruns its orthography; only the capital distinguishes the restored form from the input.

domains.title: Poet, Shapeshifter
domains.subtitle: The Radiant Brow, Chief of Bards
domains.lead: Taliesin is the supreme bard of Welsh tradition — twice-born master of the awen, the flowing spirit of poetic inspiration. As Gwion Bach he stirred Ceridwen's cauldron and caught the three drops meant for her son; as the grain the black hen swallowed he was reborn from the water with a brow so radiant that Elffin ap Gwyddno named him for it. Before Maelgwn Gwynedd's court he silenced the assembled bards with a puff of breath and freed his foster-father from thirteen locks; and behind the legend stands a historical poet of sixth-century Rheged, whose praise-songs to Urien the Historia Brittonum already knew. Poet and shapeshifter, child of the cauldron and voice of all he has ever been, Taliesin is the Welsh tradition's own answer to what a name is: a brow made radiant by what has passed through it.

cards.name: The Cauldron of Awen
cards.desc: Ceridwen's cauldron, boiled a year and a day for her son Afagddu, from which the whole science of poetry was to distill — the vessel of inspiration at the root of the legend.

cards.name: The Three Drops
cards.desc: The three drops of the cauldron's liquor that flew onto Gwion Bach's thumb as he stirred: all the awen there was, spent at once, and the reason everything after belongs to him.

cards.name: The Grain and the Hen
cards.desc: The last shape of the pursuit: Gwion as a single grain on the winnowing floor, Ceridwen as a black hen who swallowed him — the meal that became a womb.

cards.name: The Weir of Gwyddno
cards.desc: Elffin's salmon weir where the coracle came to rest: the luckless boy lifting from the water a child with a radiant brow, and giving Welsh poetry its name.

symbols.name: The cauldron of inspiration
symbols.meaning: The vessel Ceridwen set to boil for a year and a day — the awen made material, the source from which all poetry in the legend flows

symbols.name: The three drops
symbols.meaning: The sum of the cauldron's virtue, caught on a boy's thumb — inspiration as a finite, transferable grace

symbols.name: The black hen
symbols.meaning: Ceridwen's final shape in the chase — the goddess as the mother who must swallow to give birth

symbols.name: The coracle in the weir
symbols.meaning: The skin boat Elffin found among the salmon — the poet's second arrival, from the water like every gift of Annwn

symbols.name: The silenced bards
symbols.meaning: Maelgwn's court poets reduced to droning 'blerwm blerwm' by a child's breath — the power of true song over mere office

mythology.lead: Taliesin's dossier divides into two figures the Welsh tradition never quite separated: the historical poet of sixth-century Rheged, and the wonder-child of the cauldron whose story is medieval but survives whole only in sixteenth-century manuscripts. The first is attested within three centuries of his life; the second is the fullest legendary biography any Celtic poet ever received. Between them the name becomes a theory of poetry itself.

myths.title: The Poet of Urien
myths.text:
The Historia Brittonum (c. 829) names five poets famed in the days of Ida of Bernicia, in the mid-sixth century: Talhaearn Tad Awen, Aneirin, Cian, Blwchfardd — 'and Taliesin, who is renowned in British poetry'. The Book of Taliesin preserves the substance behind the notice: a core of praise-poems to Urien of Rheged and his son Owain, court verse of the Old North, singing the wars of Rheged against the Bernician Angles. Ifor Williams's scholarship established the canon: a dozen poems of the Book stand as plausibly the work of a real Taliesin, court bard of Urien in the generation before Rheged fell.

This is the oldest Taliesin the record offers — not a wonder-child but a professional of the northern courts, remembered three centuries later as the very type of the famed poet. The legend did not invent him; it annexed him, and gave the court bard of Rheged a second birth out of a goddess's cauldron.

myths.title: The Cauldron and the Chase
myths.text:
Ceridwen, dwelling by Lake Tegid in the land of Gwynedd, had two children: Creirwy the fairest of maidens and Afagddu, called Morfran, the most ill-favored of men. To compensate her dark son she set a cauldron of inspiration and science to boil for a year and a day, put blind Morda to tend the fire, and set the boy Gwion Bach to stir. On the last day three drops of the charmed liquor flew from the cauldron onto Gwion's thumb; scalded, he put it in his mouth — and at once knew all things past and to come. The cauldron split, and all its virtue was spent on the wrong child.

What follows is the great transformation chase of Celtic literature. Gwion fled as a hare; Ceridwen pursued as a greyhound. He became a fish in the river; she came after as an otter. He rose as a bird; she stooped as a hawk. At last he dropped as a single grain onto a winnowing floor, and she came as a black hen and swallowed him. Nine months she bore him, and could not kill so fair a child when he was born; she sewed him in a skin coracle and cast him into the sea on the eve of May Day.

myths.title: The Weir and the Court of Maelgwn
myths.text:
The coracle drifted into the salmon weir of Gwyddno Garanhir at the mouth of the Dyfi, where Gwyddno's son Elffin — the luckless, whose every venture failed — drew it from the water. Opening the skin, he saw a child's forehead shining from the folds and cried: 'behold a radiant brow!' — tal iesin — and so named him. The infant, not yet weaned, answered with his first poem, the Consolation of Elffin, and from that day Elffin's luck turned.

Years later, when Elffin boasted at Maelgwn Gwynedd's court that he had a wife more virtuous and a bard more skilled than any there, Maelgwn cast him into prison with thirteen locks and sent Rhun to test the wife; Rhun returned with a drugged servant-maid's finger and ring as false proof of her fall. Taliesin came to court, sat in a corner, put a finger to his lips and blew — 'blerwm blerwm' — and all the king's bards could only drone the same, save Heinin their chief. Then the child stood and sang, summoned a wind that shook the court and terrified the king, exposed the false finger, vindicated Elffin's wife, and sang the locks open. Elffin walked free, and Taliesin foretold the very end of the world.

myths.tag: Book of Taliesin: Cad Goddeu; Preiddeu Annwfn
myths.title: I Have Been in Many Shapes
myths.text:
The legendary poems of the Book give Taliesin the widest voice in Celtic literature. In Cad Goddeu, the Battle of the Trees, he boasts of a hundred existences — sword in hand, rain in the sky, string of a harp, word among letters, eagle on the tide — while Gwydion enchants the trees of the wood to march and fight for the sons of Dôn. The poem's refrain is the poet's creed: I have been in many shapes before I attained a congenial form.

In Preiddeu Annwfn, the Spoils of Annwn, he is the one survivor who can tell of Arthur's raid on the Otherworld for the cauldron of the Head of Annwn — the cauldron kindled by the breath of nine maidens, rimmed with pearls, that will not boil a coward's food. Three full shiploads went into Annwn; save seven, none returned. The poet who has been everything is the one who may speak of everything — and the two poems together are why medieval Wales called him not merely bard but Chief of Bards.

lore.syncretism: Taliesin's closest kin is Irish. The Song of Amairgen — 'I am the wind on the sea, I am the wave of the sea, I am the stag of seven tines' — speaks in the same grammar of self-predication as Cad Goddeu, and Sjoestedt set the two side by side as the Celtic poet's native form: the boast that is a cosmology, the claim that the inspired singer has been all things and so may speak of all. The awen itself has its Irish counterpart in imbas, the 'great knowledge' of the filid, and the transformation chase of the Hanes belongs to the international tale-type of the flight in shifting shapes. Within Wales, Taliesin was paired from early on with Myrddin: the Black Book of Carmarthen's Ymddiddan Myrddin a Thaliesin stages the two prophets in dialogue over the battle of Arfderydd — the two great names of Welsh poetry reading each other's grief. The Christian scribes needed no euhemerism for him: a poet, however marvelous, was safe to keep, and they kept him whole.
lore.culturalLegacy: Taliesin entered the modern world with Lady Charlotte Guest's Mabinogion (1838–49), which first printed the Hanes Taliesin from Elis Gruffydd's sixteenth-century chronicle and made the cauldron story a classic far beyond Wales. Twentieth-century scholarship restored the historical poet: Ifor Williams's Canu Taliesin (1960) separated the Urien corpus from the legendary Book and set the standard for all later work. Robert Graves's The White Goddess (1948) built a famous and much-contested mythology on Cad Goddeu — scholars reject his tree-alphabet, but he carried the poem to a vast new readership. Modern Druidry took the awen for its own: the three rays are its emblem and the word its name for inspiration. The name itself passed into architecture — Frank Lloyd Wright named his Wisconsin home and school Taliesin — and in Wales it never needed reviving: Taliesin remains a living given name, and Swansea's arts centre bears it. Few figures in the lexicon bridge a sixth-century court and a modern concert hall so completely.
lore.extendedMeditation: Taliesin is the one figure in the Celtic dossier whose myth is a complete theory of art. Inspiration exists: it is real, finite, and brewable — a cauldron's worth, a year and a day in the making. It is unjust: meant for the ill-favored son of a goddess, it lands on the thumb of a hired boy, and no pursuit, however divine, can win it back. And it is total: once swallowed, it remakes both the swallower and the swallowed, and what is reborn is not a boy with a gift but a poet who has been everything — sword and rain, eagle and grain — because poetry is exactly the faculty of having been everything. The name keeps the whole doctrine in two words: radiant brow, the visible mark where the three drops passed through. Taliesin asks the question every bard answers nightly: not whether the gift is deserved, but what it costs to carry a light on the forehead that anyone can see.
lore.originalScriptNote: The name is attested in medieval Welsh manuscripts in the Latin alphabet — the Book of Taliesin (NLW Peniarth MS 2) for the poems, and the sixteenth-century chronicle of Elis Gruffydd for the full legend — and the spelling Taliesin is already plain ASCII: no diacritic, no distinctive letter, so the restoration is a matter of canonical reference rather than rescued orthography. Because the name is pure ASCII, its domain was registered decades ago in the ordinary way: taliesin.com is held by a third party outside the PuniCodex collection and is watched for release — no form of the name is currently owned, and this temple claims none.

lore.archaeology: Taliesin is a wholly textual figure: no inscription names him, no ogham stone or cross-slab invokes him, and the Welsh epigraphic record — Romano-British memorial stones and the ogham stones of the Irish settlers in Dyfed — belongs to other names entirely. His witnesses are manuscripts of unusually late but exact pedigree. The Book of Taliesin (NLW Peniarth MS 2, early fourteenth century) preserves both the sixth-century praise-poems to Urien of Rheged and the legendary cycle in a single hand. The Black Book of Carmarthen (mid-thirteenth century) holds the Ymddiddan Myrddin a Thaliesin. The Historia Brittonum's notice travels in its ninth-century recensions, Harley MS 3859 chief among them. And the full legendary biography, the Hanes Taliesin, survives entire only in the sixteenth-century chronicle of Elis Gruffydd — a late witness to a story whose own materials (the Triads, the Book's persona-poems) prove medieval. Between Peniarth and Gruffydd stands the whole transmission: a poet who is historical, legendary, and manuscript all at once.
